Adaptive Minds: Empowering Agents with LoRA-as-Tools

Pavan C Shekar ††thanks: QpiAI.Tech, Bengaluru, India. pavan.s@qpiai.tech Affiliation: QpiAI.Tech Affiliation: Bengaluru, India    Ashwanth Krishnan ††thanks: QpiAI.Tech, Bengaluru, India. ashwanth.krishnan@qpiai.tech Affiliation: QpiAI.Tech Affiliation: Bengaluru, India
Abstract

We present Adaptive Minds, an agentic system that treats LoRA adapters as domain-specific tools. Instead of relying on a single fine-tuned model or rigid rule-based routing, our approach empowers the base LLM itself to act as a semantic router analyzing each query and dynamically selecting the most relevant LoRA tool. This enables the agent to seamlessly switch between different domain experts on demand. By combining the flexibility of multi-agent orchestration with the efficiency of parameter-efficient fine-tuning, Adaptive Minds delivers accurate, specialized responses while preserving conversational ability. The system is built with LangGraph for workflow management, supports both API and web interfaces, and is fully open source, providing a scalable and extensible foundation for domain-adaptive AI assistance. Code: https://github.com/qpiai/adaptive-minds

   

Keywords Multi-agent systems ⋅\cdot Domain-specific AI ⋅\cdot LoRA fine-tuning ⋅\cdot Semantic routing ⋅\cdot Agentic AI frameworks ⋅\cdot Parameter-efficient fine-tuning ⋅\cdot Tool-augmented LLMs

1 Introduction

The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding and generation. However, while general-purpose models excel at broad knowledge tasks, they often lack the depth and specificity required for specialized domains such as chemistry, medicine, or finance. Traditional approaches to domain specialization typically involve either training separate models from scratch or fine-tuning entire models for each domain, both of which are computationally expensive and resource-intensive.

Recent developments in parameter-efficient fine-tuning, particularly Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [1], have made it feasible to create domain-specific adaptations of large models with minimal computational overhead. However, a critical challenge remains: how to intelligently route user queries to the most appropriate domain expert while maintaining system coherence and user experience[2].

This paper introduces Adaptive Minds, an agentic system that addresses this challenge through AI-powered intelligent routing. Our key contributions are:

  • •

    LoRA-as-Tools: A unified framework where specialized LoRA adapters are dynamically selected and applied as needed.

  • •

    Semantic Routing: The base model performs query analysis and routes to the right domain adapter without handcrafted rules or keyword matching.

  • •

    Modular Multi-Agent Design: Built with LangGraph, separating routing from expertise for scalability and extensibility.

  • •

    Visible Routing Decisions: The system outputs the chosen domain adapter for each query, providing transparency into how requests are directed.

  • •

    Open Source System: Full implementation with Docker, API, and web interfaces for easy deployment.

2 Related Work

2.1 Multi-Agent Systems for NLP

Multi-agent systems have been extensively studied in artificial intelligence, with recent applications to natural language processing showing promising results [3, 4]. Traditional multi-agent NLP systems often rely on predefined rules or simple classification models for task routing. Our approach differs by using the base language model itself as the routing intelligence, leveraging its semantic understanding capabilities.

2.2 Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, particularly LoRA [1] and its variants [5, 6], have revolutionized domain adaptation for large language models. While most work focuses on individual domain adaptations, our system demonstrates how multiple LoRA adapters can be orchestrated within a single multi-agent framework.

2.3 Domain-Specific Language Models

Previous work on domain-specific language models includes BioBERT [7], FinBERT [8], and ChemBERTa [9] for medical, financial, and chemical domains respectively. These models typically require full fine-tuning and operate independently. Our approach enables multiple domain experts to coexist within a unified system with shared computational resources.

2.4 Intelligent Task Routing

Task routing in multi-agent systems has been addressed through various approaches including reinforcement learning [10], classification-based routing [11], and rule-based systems [12]. Our AI-semantic routing represents a novel approach that leverages the language understanding capabilities of the base model for routing decisions[13, 14].

3 Methodology

3.1 System Architecture

Adaptive Minds is structured around two main agents (Router Agent + Expert Agent) orchestrated via LangGraph. While in our experiments we used a LLaMA-3.1 8B base model and five domain adapters, the architecture is designed to support any base model and any existing LoRA adapters, and allows you to train and add new ones seamlessly.

3.1.1 Router Agent

The Router Agent is responsible for analyzing incoming queries and selecting the most appropriate domain expert. Unlike traditional routing approaches that rely on keyword matching or separate classification models, our Router Agent leverages the base LLM’s semantic understanding to perform domain inference.

Routing Process:
  1. 1.

    Query Analysis: The router receives a user query and constructs a structured prompt containing the query and available domain experts.

  2. 2.

    Semantic Evaluation: The base model analyzes the query semantically, considering context, intent, and domain relevance.

  3. 3.

    Domain Selection: The model returns the name (or identifier) of the chosen adapter/domain.

  4. 4.

    Validation and Fallback: If the choice is ambiguous or invalid, the system can validate the output (e.g. match against a canonical adapter list) and fall back to a safe default (e.g. a “General” adapter).

Routing Prompt Template:

Adaptive Minds does not use a hardcoded routing prompt. Instead, the Router Agent maintains metadata about each registered LoRA adapter (e.g. domain name, description, instructions, keywords) in a configuration file. When the system is started, the router dynamically builds its routing prompt from the metadata file.

This approach makes routing logic flexible, maintainable, and scalable. You can add, remove, or update domain adapters by modifying configuration metadata—without touching the core router code.

Example Prompt:
Analyze this user query and select the most appropriate
domain expert to handle it.

Query: "{query}"

Available Domain Experts:
- General - For casual conversation, greetings,
  general knowledge, everyday questions
- Chemistry - For chemical compounds, reactions,
  molecules, laboratory procedures
- Finance - For money, investments, stocks,
  banking, economics, trading
- AI/GPT - For artificial intelligence, machine
  learning, programming, algorithms
- Medical - For health, diseases, treatments,
  symptoms, anatomy, medicine

Instructions:
- Analyze the query carefully
- Consider the main topic and intent
- Choose the domain expert that best matches the query
- If unsure or the query is general/casual,
  choose General
- Respond with ONLY the domain name

Note: In our experiments, we used LLaMA-3.1 8B Instruct as the base LLM and five LoRA adapters corresponding to the domains above. However, the system is not limited to this setup: you can plug in any base model, use pretrained LoRAs, or train new LoRAs for custom domains, and the router logic will apply similarly.

We also experimented (empirically) with alternative routing mechanisms such as keyword-based matching and hybrid (keyword + semantic) routing, but found that unconstrained semantic routing by the base LLM yielded more consistent and reliable domain choices.

3.1.2 Expert Agent

The Expert Agent generates domain-specific responses using the selected LoRA adapter. Each domain expert is implemented as a LoRA adaptation of the base Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct model, fine-tuned on domain-specific datasets.

Response Generation Process:
  1. 1.

    Adapter Loading: The system loads the appropriate LoRA adapter for the selected domain.

  2. 2.

    Context Integration: Conversation history is incorporated to maintain context continuity.

  3. 3.

    Prompt Formatting: Domain-specific prompt templates optimize response generation.

  4. 4.

    Response Generation: The adapted model generates a specialized response.

3.2 Domain Expert Implementation

3.2.1 LoRA Adapter Configuration

In our design, each domain expert is realized as a LoRA adapter, which is applied on top of a shared base model (e.g., Llama 3.1-8B). This arrangement allows us to maintain a single backbone while specializing behavior via lightweight adapters.

Mathematically, each LoRA adapter introduces a low-rank update to the original weight matrix WW of the base model layer. Instead of updating all parameters, LoRA represents the change as the product of two smaller matrices AA and BB scaled by a factor α\alpha:

W′=W+Δ​W,Δ​W=α⋅B​A,W^{\prime}=W+\Delta W,\qquad\Delta W=\alpha\cdot BA, (1)

where A∈ℝr×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} and B∈ℝd×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} with r≪dr\ll d. This low-rank decomposition significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters while preserving expressive capacity.

We store each adapter in a Hugging Face repository, and associate with it descriptive metadata and a domain-specific system prompt to steer the adapter’s behavior.

3.2.2 Domain Specializations and Dataset Foundations

Each domain expert is fine-tuned (via LoRA) on a curated dataset reflecting its specialization. Below, we describe each domain’s role and the dataset used:

General Expert

The General adapter is fine-tuned on mhenrichsen/alpaca_2k_test, a 2K-sample instruction dataset spanning a wide variety of everyday tasks and Q&A styles. This domain acts as a fallback for conversational queries or when domain identification is uncertain.

Chemistry Expert

For chemistry, we adopt the AI4Chem/ChemData700K dataset, which contains 700,000 chemistry-oriented instruction/response pairs. The adapter learns to reason about molecules, reactions, safety protocols, and laboratory practices, enabling it to deliver precise chemical explanations and analyses.

AI / Technology Expert

The pavan01729/GPT_AI_5.0_alpaca dataset provides content focused on machine learning, algorithms, system design, and code. This adapter is tailored for technical queries, giving it fluency in programming language reasoning and algorithmic discourse.

Finance Expert

We use gbharti/finance-alpaca as the finance domain dataset. It comprises prompts, analyses, and insights related to economics, markets, financial planning, and investment forecasting. The adapter learns domain-specific vocabulary and reasoning patterns of financial discourse.

Medical Expert

The medical adapter is trained on Kabatubare/medical-alpaca, a medically centered dataset capturing disease information, diagnostics, treatment discussion, and guidelines. Because of the sensitive nature of medical advice, this adapter is also configured to embed disclaimers or encourage consulting professionals when appropriate.

By aligning each domain adapter to a high-quality, domain-specific dataset, we give each expert a specialized footing in its area. During inference, the system activates only the selected adapter, leveraging its focused capability without requiring full re-training of the base model.

3.3 LangGraph Workflow Implementation

Adaptive Minds employs LangGraph [15] as the underlying framework for workflow orchestration and process management. LangGraph provides a structured yet flexible way to define and execute agent workflows, enabling the system to coordinate routing, inference, and memory components efficiently. It manages the conversation state across multiple interactions, ensuring that contextual information is consistently preserved and accessible throughout the dialogue. Furthermore, its robust error-handling and fallback mechanisms improve reliability by allowing the system to recover gracefully from failed operations. LangGraph’s modular design also facilitates rapid experimentation and extensibility—new nodes, agents, or workflows can be introduced without disrupting existing functionality. In addition, its built-in logging and monitoring tools provide transparency and traceability across agent decisions, making it an ideal backbone for scalable, interpretable, and adaptive AI systems.

While LangGraph serves as the primary orchestration framework in this implementation, the workflow design of Adaptive Minds is framework-agnostic and can be replicated using other agent frameworks or even through custom orchestration logic without relying on any dedicated agent framework.

3.4 Conversation Memory and Context

To ensure continuity and coherence in dialogue, Adaptive Minds incorporates a structured conversation memory mechanism. The system retains a selective history of recent user–assistant exchanges, allowing each new query to be interpreted in the context of prior interactions. During inference, the router and expert modules integrate this contextual information directly into their prompts, enabling more accurate and contextually grounded responses. Memory length is dynamically managed to balance contextual richness with computational efficiency—older, less relevant turns are pruned to maintain optimal performance. This design ensures that the model remains responsive and context-aware without incurring excessive memory or latency overhead.

4 Experimental Setup

We conducted all experiments on a single NVIDIA L40s GPU, using the Meta LLaMA 3.1-8B-Instruct as the base model (8 billion parameters, 128 K token context length, 16-bit precision). The system was fully orchestrated in this environment to ensure consistency and reproducibility.

For domain adaptation, we used LoRA with rank = 16, α=32\alpha=32, and dropout = 0.1, applied to the query, key, value, and output projection layers. Each domain-specific adapter was fine-tuned via QpiAI Pro, a no-code platform that enables rapid prototyping through seamless dataset creation, fine-tuning, and deployment of LLMs and Vision models. The training datasets used were:

  • •

    Chemistry: AI4Chem/ChemData700K

  • •

    Finance: gbharti/finance-alpaca

  • •

    AI/Technology: pavan01729/GPT_AI_5.0_alpaca

  • •

    Medical: Kabatubare/medical-alpaca

  • •

    General: mhenrichsen/alpaca_2k_test

For deployment, the system is packaged in a containerized architecture to support portability and reproducibility. The backend is implemented in FastAPI, responsible for query processing, routing, and adapter orchestration. The frontend is built in Streamlit for interactive use. The full stack is deployed via Docker with GPU support (using the NVIDIA Container Toolkit). At startup, the base model and all LoRA adapters are preloaded; adapter switching incurs negligible overhead. We include automated downloading, caching, and versioning of adapters and base models from Hugging Face repositories.

4.1 Deployment Requirements

The system requires a GPU with at least 16 GB of VRAM, 16 GB or more of system RAM, and a minimum of 30 GB of available storage for model files. On the software side, the deployment environment should include Docker with GPU support, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and Python 3.10 or later. These specifications ensure smooth model loading, adapter switching, and real-time inference performance.

5 Use Cases and Applications

To illustrate the flexibility and real-world potential of the Adaptive Minds framework, we present several representative use cases. These examples show how the system can adapt across domains and evolve over time.

5.1 Representative Scenarios

Multi-Domain Virtual Assistant

An organization wants a single intelligent assistant that can handle questions in HR, finance, product support, legal, and technical domains. Rather than building separate bots, Adaptive Minds lets the assistant route queries to the appropriate LoRA adapter (e.g., “HR”, “Finance”, “Technical”) and respond with domain-aware expertise. As new departments or topics emerge, new adapters can be trained and added without changing the core system.

Support Desk for SaaS / Enterprise Tools

In a software product support setting, users might ask about billing, feature usage, integration issues, bug diagnostics, or account settings. Adaptive Minds routes each ticket or chat query to the right adapter (e.g., “Billing / Finance”, “Product / Usage”, “Technical / Debugging”) to provide accurate, context-sensitive answers. As the product evolves, additional adapters (e.g., “Analytics”, “Security”) can be incorporated seamlessly.

Educational Tutoring System

A tutoring platform supports multiple school subjects (mathematics, chemistry, biology, computer science, history). When a student poses a question, Adaptive Minds identifies and activates the corresponding subject LoRA (e.g., “Math”, “Chemistry”) to produce a precise explanation. When a new subject is added (e.g., economics), a new adapter can be trained and integrated into the system without altering routing logic.

Healthcare / Clinical Assistant

A medical assistant can handle general medical questions, pharmacology, radiology, nutrition, mental health, and more. A query about drug interactions routes to a pharmacology adapter; one about imaging routes to radiology; one about symptoms to general clinical. As new specialties (e.g., cardiology or oncology) are added, new LoRAs for those can join the system.

Finance & Investment Advisory

A financial advisory assistant may receive questions spanning macroeconomics, portfolio strategy, taxation, cryptocurrency, retirement planning, or ESG investing. Adaptive Minds routes each query to the corresponding financial adapter (e.g., “Portfolio”, “Tax / Legal”, “Crypto”) to provide expert insights. As new financial domains emerge (e.g., derivatives, sustainable investing), new adapters can be trained and plugged in.

5.2 Key Takeaways from Use Cases

These scenarios highlight several important strengths:

  • •

    Domain Agnostic Routing: The system can route to many kinds of domain adapters (finance, education, health, etc.) depending only on query semantics.

  • •

    Modular Growth: New adapters can be trained and added to the system without modifying routing logic or rewriting existing modules.

  • •

    Adaptive Expertise: The assistant can switch between expert modules dynamically, delivering specialist responses while maintaining conversational flow.

  • •

    Unified Infrastructure: A single backbone model supports all domains, reducing duplication and enabling efficient resource use.

In summary, Adaptive Minds offers a flexible and scalable backbone for agents that must operate across many domains, grow with new specializations, and deliver precise knowledge as needed.

6 Evaluation Metrics

We assess the system along five key dimensions:

  • •

    Routing Accuracy: The fraction of queries correctly routed to the intended domain expert.

  • •

    Response Quality: Human judgments of how relevant and accurate the generated answers are.

  • •

    Latency: End-to-end elapsed time from user query to model response.

  • •

    Memory Footprint: GPU memory usage during inference.

  • •

    Domain Coverage: The breadth of topics each domain expert can handle reliably.

6.1 Baseline Methods

We compare our method against several baselines to contextualize gains:

  • •

    Single Model: A general LLaMA-3.1-8B instance without any domain adapters.

  • •

    Keyword Routing: A rule-based router that counts domain keywords in the query.

  • •

    Hybrid AI + Keyword: Combines semantic routing with keyword signals.

  • •

    Random Routing: Routes queries randomly to one of the domain experts.

7 Results

7.1 Routing Performance

We evaluated routing accuracy using a curated test set of 25 queries spanning all five domains (5 queries per domain), with varying difficulty levels (easy, medium, hard). Our AI-semantic routing approach achieved perfect accuracy:

The system demonstrated perfect domain classification across all query types, with zero confusion between domains. This validates that AI-semantic routing, leveraging the base model’s natural language understanding, can reliably identify domain intent without rule-based constraints.

7.1.1 Comparison with Keyword-Based Routing

To validate the effectiveness of our AI-semantic routing approach, we compared it against a traditional keyword-based routing baseline. The keyword router counts domain-specific keyword occurrences in queries and routes to the domain with the highest match count (defaulting to the General domain when no keywords are detected).

These results show that AI-semantic routing significantly outperforms keyword matching across all domains, with the most substantial gains in specialized domains (Medical: +80.0%, AI: +66.7%). While keyword matching achieved 100% accuracy on General domain queries (since conversational keywords often map to general topics), it struggled on domain-specific inputs (e.g. Medical 20.0%, AI 33.3%).

We identified several root causes for keyword matching failures:

  1. 1.

    Ambiguous keywords: Terms like “bond” or “compound” may map to multiple domains, leading to incorrect routing.

  2. 2.

    Absence of explicit keywords: Some queries (e.g., “What causes a common cold?”) lack domain keywords yet are clearly medical.

  3. 3.

    False partial matches: Substrings like “hi” in “high blood pressure” may incorrectly trigger general domain routing.

  4. 4.

    Multi-word phrase blindness: Phrases like “machine learning” or “neural network” may not be matched as semantic units, hurting keyword coverage.

In addition, keyword matching performance degrades sharply with query complexity (medium and hard queries). In contrast, our AI-semantic router achieved perfect accuracy across all difficulty levels, demonstrating robustness to variation in phrasing and complexity.

Implications: The results validate our architectural choice to use LLM-based semantic routing over simpler rule-based methods. Although keyword matching adds negligible latency, its poor accuracy (48.3%) would degrade user experience in real settings. The extra 0.1–0.3 s cost of AI routing is justified by a 2.1× accuracy improvement, delivering production-level reliability with perfect routing.

7.2 System Performance and Latency Analysis

We benchmarked end-to-end system performance across 20 sequential queries, measuring response times, resource utilization, and comparing to a baseline (base model without LoRA).

Counter-intuitively, although adding a routing step might incur overhead, Adaptive Minds is 3.1× faster in mean latency than the baseline (10.807 s → 3.486 s). This performance gain arises from the efficiency of domain-specialized LoRA generation.

Explanation of Performance Gain

The observed speedup stems from:

1. Focused Generation: Domain adapters produce concise, structured responses and often complete generation faster. 2. Token Efficiency: Unlike the baseline which often saturates the token limit and produces verbose output, LoRA adapters average 100–400 tokens and stop naturally. 3. Learned Response Patterns: Fine-tuning conditions the model to produce domain-appropriate answer lengths and better EOS decisions, reducing redundancy.

The General domain had the fastest mean latency, while Medical domain was the slowest (due to complexity and disclaimers). Nonetheless, even in Medical, performance still outperformed the baseline by about 2×.

7.3 Cold Start vs. Warm Start Performance

We measured latency differences between cold start (first query after context clearance) and warm start (subsequent queries):

Warm-start queries benefit from cached model states, tokenizer warm-up, and context reuse, leading to a 36.9% latency reduction. This suggests multi-turn dialogues become significantly more efficient after the first turn.

7.4 Resource Utilization

Despite supporting five LoRA adapters simultaneously, Adaptive Minds adds only a minimal memory overhead compared to the base model. On an NVIDIA L40s GPU, total memory usage increased from 14.96 GB for the base model to 15.12 GB with all adapters loaded—an overhead of just 0.16 GB (approximately 1.1%). This efficiency underscores the compact design of LoRA, where only low-rank parameter matrices are added instead of duplicating the entire model, enabling multi-domain specialization with negligible GPU footprint.

Other Metrics: The router decision time ranged between 0.1–0.3 s, which is already included in the total response latency. Adapter switching overhead was negligible since all LoRA adapters were pre-loaded at startup. The system achieved a throughput of approximately 20 queries per minute on a single GPU (sequential execution), with CPU utilization between 12–18% during inference.

7.5 Efficiency Analysis: Adaptive Minds Overhead

Routing overhead is a common worry in multi-agent systems. We decompose total latency:

- Router inference: 0.1–0.3 s — semantic domain selection - Expert generation: 2.0–5.0 s — domain-specific output - Overhead: prompt formatting, memory, post-processing

Net Effect: while routing adds a small overhead, the gains from focused LoRA generation produce a net speedup of 7.3 s ( 67.7% latency reduction) compared to the baseline. This confirms that intelligent routing combined with adapted specialists is not only more accurate but also substantially more efficient than a monolithic model.

7.6 Qualitative Observations

Beyond metrics, we observed:

1. Response Conciseness: LoRA outputs were more focused and domain-relevant, avoiding tangential digressions. 2. Contextual Appropriateness: Chemistry answers included formulas and safety notes; Medical answers had disclaimers; Finance used domain vocabulary — all without post-editing. 3. Routing Transparency: The system clearly states which expert handled each query, improving interpretability and user trust. 4. Zero Routing Errors: Across all 25 test queries, no routing mistakes occurred, even on ambiguous inputs.

Key Findings Summary
  • •

    Perfect routing accuracy (100% over 25 queries)

  • •

    3.1× average speedup compared to baseline

  • •

    Minimal memory overhead (+1.1%) for 5 LoRA adapters

  • •

    Consistent domain performance with no routing errors

  • •

    Warm start yields 36.9% improvement over cold start

8 Discussion

8.1 Advantages of AI-Semantic Routing

Our AI-semantic routing approach offers several key advantages:

  • •

    Contextual Understanding: Unlike keyword-based approaches, semantic routing considers context and intent, leading to more accurate domain selection.

  • •

    No Additional Training: The routing mechanism leverages the existing capabilities of the base model without requiring separate training data or models.

  • •

    Adaptability: The system can handle novel query types and edge cases that might not be covered by rule-based approaches.

  • •

    Transparency: The selected domain adapter is revealed for each query, providing a minimal form of routing transparency.

  • •

    Pure AI Superiority: Our experiments revealed that pure AI-semantic routing outperformed hybrid approaches that attempted to combine AI analysis with keyword matching. The base language model’s semantic understanding is sophisticated enough that additional rule-based constraints actually hinder rather than help the routing decision process.

8.2 Scalability and Extensibility

The architecture of Adaptive Minds is built to be highly scalable and flexible. You can swap in any base model, integrate existing LoRA adapters simply by referencing them, or train new adapters and plug them into the system—all without touching the core routing logic. The framework supports end-to-end training and deployment of new adapters, and lets organizations rapidly expand into new domains. This modularity ensures that as your needs grow, the system can evolve: more adapters, updated models, custom specializations—all coexist seamlessly within the same architecture

8.3 Limitations

Adaptive Minds demonstrates strong modularity and adaptability, but several limitations remain. First, each query requires two inference passes—one for routing and another for expert generation—which adds latency compared to a single fine-tuned model. Second, certain user queries naturally span multiple domains (e.g., pharma and chemistry), making it difficult for the system to assign a single expert without losing contextual richness. Third, as the number of concurrently loaded LoRA adapters increases, potential interference between adapters may affect stability and performance. Finally, evaluating domain-specific quality remains challenging, as it requires expert human annotation and large-scale validation to ensure fairness, reliability, and consistency across specialized domains.

8.4 Future Work

Future work will focus on enhancing both scalability and intelligence within the Adaptive Minds framework. One key direction involves enabling the system to dynamically load new LoRA adapters during the ReAct loop. In the current setup, once an expert adapter is selected, the entire response is generated using that adapter alone. By contrast, dynamic loading would allow the router to activate or switch adapters mid-inference as reasoning unfolds—similar to how an agent decides which external tool to call next. This would enable context-aware specialization, where different sections of a response could draw on different domain experts in real time. We also plan to explore weighted adapter fusion, allowing the router to assign proportional importance to multiple domains (e.g., 0.3 for Medical and 0.7 for Chemistry) for more nuanced outputs. Additional goals include reducing computational overhead through lighter or inline routing, and investigating caching and quantization strategies for efficient on-demand adapter loading. Finally, we will expand evaluation to larger multi-domain benchmarks and incorporate transparency features that display which adapters contributed to each output. Together, these efforts aim to make Adaptive Minds more adaptive, memory-efficient, and responsive to complex, interdisciplinary queries[2].

9 Conclusion

We introduced Adaptive Minds, an agentic framework that treats LoRA adapters as modular tools the base LLM can call on demand. Rather than building many specialized monolithic models or brittle rule systems, the backbone LLM acts as a semantic router: it inspects each query and dynamically selects the most appropriate LoRA tool to handle it. This lets the system combine focused, expert knowledge with natural conversational behavior, so users get specialist answers without losing dialogue quality.

The key strength of Adaptive Minds is its flexibility and scalability. The architecture is model-agnostic — it can run with any base model, ingest existing LoRA adapters, and support training and registration of new adapters without changing the core routing logic. This design unlocks many real-world use cases (enterprise assistants, tutoring, healthcare triage, finance, research aids, etc.) while keeping compute and storage efficient through parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Our LangGraph-based implementation, together with API and web interfaces and an open-source codebase, provides a practical, extensible foundation for deploying domain-adaptive agents.
